$comment: Entity copy (HB-156): short human-written paragraphs the page generator reads, keyed by core ids. Facts live in the core; the one place note letters are quoted (each tuning's open strings, low to high) is checked against the core by test/entity-copy.spec.ts. Drafts by agent; the founder edits.

chords.major: The major triad is the root, a major third and a fifth, and it is the sound most other chords are measured against. On the neck it appears as the same compact shape in many places, because the three notes repeat on every string set. Its nearest relatives are the minor triad, one note lower in the middle, and the major seventh, one note taller.
chords.minor: The minor triad swaps the major third for a minor third and keeps the fifth, which is what gives it a darker colour. Each of its three notes repeats across the neck, so the shape you see is a map of every place it can be played. Flatten its fifth and you reach the diminished triad; stack a seventh and you reach the minor seventh.
chords.5: The power chord is only a root and a fifth, with no third to say whether it is major or minor. That leaves the shape two notes wide and easy to slide along the neck. Add a third above it and it becomes one of the triads.
chords.7: The dominant seventh adds a minor seventh on top of a major triad, which leaves a restless interval pair inside it. It lives on the neck in several overlapping shapes, since its four notes repeat on every string group. Next to it sit the major seventh, with a raised top note, and the ninth, which stacks one more note above.
chords.maj7: The major seventh stacks a major seventh on top of the major triad, so the top note sits a semitone below the next root. The map shows four notes, each repeating across the neck, and the root and seventh are close neighbours wherever they land. Lower that top note and you get the dominant seventh.
chords.m7: The minor seventh is the minor triad with a minor seventh added, four notes in all. Because it contains the notes of a major chord a minor third higher, the two shapes overlap on the neck. It is a close cousin of the half diminished chord, which differs only by a flattened fifth.
chords.mmaj7: The minor major seventh joins a minor triad to a major seventh, an unusual pairing of a dark middle and a bright top. Its four notes repeat across the neck like any other seventh chord, with the root and seventh sitting a semitone apart. Lower the seventh by a semitone and you are back at the minor seventh.
chords.6: The sixth chord adds a major sixth to the major triad, giving four notes with no seventh. The same notes appear in the minor seventh chord a sixth higher, so the neck shows two names for one shape. It sits between the plain major triad and the major seventh.
chords.m6: The minor sixth adds a major sixth to the minor triad, which keeps the dark third and lifts the top note. Its four notes repeat across the neck and share a shape with the half diminished chord on a different root. It sits next to the minor triad and the minor seventh.
chords.add9: The added ninth places a ninth above a major triad and skips the seventh entirely. On the neck the ninth is the same note as the second, so it can appear right next to the root. Compare it with the ninth chord, which adds a seventh underneath.
chords.2: The added second is a major triad with the second degree stacked in, and it keeps the fifth. The second sits close to the root and the third, so the shape is tight wherever it appears. It is the nearest relative of the suspended second, which drops the third.
chords.6-9: The six nine chord puts a major sixth and a ninth over a major triad, with the seventh left out. The fifth is optional, so some shapes on the neck leave it out. It is a neighbour of the sixth chord and the added ninth, each of which holds one of its extra notes.
chords.m6-9: The minor six nine chord combines a minor third with a major sixth and a ninth. The fifth is optional, so the map marks it as one you may leave out. Compare it with the minor sixth, which holds just the sixth, and the minor added ninth, which holds just the ninth.
chords.madd9: The minor added ninth places a ninth above a minor triad and leaves out the seventh. The ninth sits one step above the root, so it can sit right beside it on the neck. Its relatives are the minor triad and the minor ninth chord.
chords.add9no3: This chord is a root, a fifth and a ninth, with no third. Without it, the shape is neither major nor minor and can sit under either. It is a spacious relative of the added ninth and the suspended second.
chords.sus4: The suspended fourth swaps the third for a fourth, so the chord leans toward resolving. The fourth is only a step above the third, which means the two shapes sit very close on the neck. It is a near cousin of the suspended second, which pulls the middle note down instead.
chords.sus2: The suspended second replaces the third with a second and keeps the fifth, which opens the chord up. The second is an octave away from the ninth, so its shape resembles the added ninth without the third. It is the mirror of the suspended fourth, which moves the middle note upward.
chords.7sus4: This chord takes the dominant seventh and swaps its third for a fourth. That leaves a suspended fourth with a minor seventh on top. On the neck it overlaps with the shapes of its two parents, the suspended fourth and the dominant seventh.
chords.9: The ninth chord is a dominant seventh with a ninth stacked above it, five notes in its full form. The fifth is optional, so many neck shapes leave it out. Its nearest relatives are the dominant seventh below it and the eleventh and thirteenth above.
chords.maj9: The major ninth is a major seventh chord with a ninth added on top. The fifth is optional, which lets the shape thin out on the neck. It sits between the major seventh and the major eleventh in the family of tall major chords.
chords.m9: The minor ninth is a minor seventh with a ninth stacked above, and the fifth is optional. Its notes repeat in several overlapping shapes on the neck. It sits between the minor seventh and the minor eleventh.
chords.mmaj9: The minor major ninth stacks a ninth over the minor major seventh, with an optional fifth. It keeps the minor third and the major seventh, so a semitone gap sits between the seventh and the root above. It is the tallest sibling of the minor major seventh.
chords.11: The eleventh chord extends a dominant ninth to the eleventh, and the map marks the third, ninth and others as optional. In practice many of its notes can be left out, so shapes on the neck range from sparse to full. It sits between the ninth and the thirteenth.
chords.maj11: The major eleventh lifts the major ninth with an eleventh on top, with the third and ninth optional. Because the eleventh falls close to the third, the full chord leans toward a suspended sound. It sits above the major ninth and below the major thirteenth.
chords.m11: The minor eleventh builds on the minor ninth by adding an eleventh above. The fifth and ninth are optional, so the shape can be reduced a long way. It is the minor side of the tall chord family.
chords.13: The thirteenth chord is the tallest of the dominant stack, running up through the seventh, ninth and eleventh to the thirteenth. On a six string neck most of the inner notes are optional, so shapes keep the root, the seventh and the thirteenth and drop the rest. Its smaller relatives are the ninth and the eleventh.
chords.maj13: The major thirteenth tops a major seventh with a thirteenth, and the ninth and eleventh are optional in the map. Only the essential notes need to sound for the chord to be recognised on the neck. It is the tall end of the major seventh family.
chords.m13: The minor thirteenth extends the minor ninth with an eleventh and a thirteenth, and those inner notes are optional. Its core of root, minor third, seventh and thirteenth appears in many places on the neck. It is the tall end of the minor seventh family.
chords.7s9: The seventh sharp nine takes the dominant seventh and adds a raised ninth, which sits right beside the major third. That close pair gives it a gritty sound, and the map shows the two notes next to each other. The fifth is optional.
chords.7b9: The seventh flat nine adds a lowered ninth to the dominant seventh, a semitone above the root. On the neck the root and the flat nine sit side by side, and the fifth is optional. It is the tense sibling of the plain ninth chord.
chords.7s5: The seventh sharp five raises the fifth of the dominant seventh by a semitone. The raised fifth sits a semitone below the sixth, so the shape resembles the augmented triad with a seventh on top. It is a close cousin of the dominant seventh and the augmented chord.
chords.7b5: The seventh flat five lowers the fifth of the dominant seventh by a semitone. It keeps the major third and the minor seventh, which form a tritone with each other. That makes the shape symmetrical in a useful way, since the same notes serve a chord a tritone away.
chords.9b5: This chord is a ninth chord with a lowered fifth, and the map marks the third as optional. The flat five and the minor seventh sit close, so the shape is compact. It sits next to the ninth and the seventh flat five.
chords.9s5: The ninth sharp five is a ninth chord with a raised fifth, and the third is optional in the map. The raised fifth sits a semitone below the sixth, and the shape is related to the augmented triad. It is a neighbour of the ninth and the seventh sharp five.
chords.9s11: The ninth sharp eleven adds a raised eleventh to the ninth chord, with the fifth optional. The raised eleventh sits a semitone above the fourth degree, so it can be close to the fifth on the neck. It is the bright version of the eleventh chord.
chords.7-6: This chord is a dominant seventh with a sixth added, and the fifth is optional. The sixth and the seventh sit a semitone apart, so they appear side by side on the neck. It is related to the dominant seventh add thirteen, which holds the same notes an octave apart.
chords.9-6: The ninth add six combines a ninth chord with a sixth, with the third and fifth optional. Its upper notes cluster in a small span, so the shape is dense in one region of the neck. It is a relative of the ninth and the seventh add six.
chords.7-13: The dominant seventh add thirteen puts a thirteenth on the dominant seventh and skips the inner notes. The thirteenth is the same note as the sixth, an octave higher, so the neck shows the shapes of the seventh add six. It is the sparse version of the thirteenth chord.
chords.11b9: This chord combines a flattened ninth with an eleventh on a dominant seventh, with the third, fifth and some others optional. The flat nine sits just above the root and the eleventh sits just above the third. It is a tense cousin of the eleventh chord.
chords.13b9: The thirteenth flat nine is a thirteenth chord with a flattened ninth. The inner notes are optional, so the core is the root, the third, the seventh, the flat nine and the thirteenth. It is the tense counterpart of the plain thirteenth.
chords.13s11: The thirteenth sharp eleven pairs a thirteenth with a raised eleventh on a dominant seventh. Several inner notes are optional, so the shape can be thin. It is the brighter relative of the plain thirteenth.
chords.13b9b5: This chord stacks a thirteenth with a flattened ninth and a flattened fifth, and several notes are optional, even the root. It is a dense altered chord, and its shapes sit in small clusters on the neck. Its parents are the thirteenth flat nine and the seventh flat five.
chords.13b9s11: This chord combines a thirteenth, a flattened ninth and a raised eleventh, and the root, third and fifth are optional. That leaves only the upper notes as essential in the map. It is one of the most altered members of the thirteenth family.
chords.b9: The seventh flat nine, listed on its own, is a dominant seventh with a lowered ninth and an optional fifth. The flat nine sits a semitone above the root on the neck. It overlaps with the diminished seventh chord shape built from the third.
chords.b9s5: This chord is a seventh flat nine with a raised fifth, and the third is optional. It joins two altered notes, one a semitone above the root and one a semitone above the fifth. Its parents are the seventh flat nine and the seventh sharp five.
chords.b9s11: This chord is a seventh flat nine with a raised eleventh, and the third and fifth are optional. The flat nine and the raised eleventh are both altered notes, one near the root and one near the fifth. It is a close relative of the seventh flat nine.
chords.b9b5: This chord is a seventh flat nine with a lowered fifth, with the third optional. The flat nine and the flat five are both altered notes, one near the root and one near the fourth. Its parents are the seventh flat nine and the seventh flat five.
chords.s9: The seventh sharp nine, listed here as its own entry, is a dominant seventh with a raised ninth and an optional fifth. The raised ninth sits a semitone below the major third, so the two sit close together on the neck. It is the gritty relative of the plain ninth chord.
chords.s11: The augmented eleventh is a ninth chord with a raised eleventh, and the third and fifth are optional. The raised eleventh sits next to the fifth, so the shape can crowd in that region. It is a close cousin of the ninth sharp eleven.
chords.maj7s5: The major seventh sharp five raises the fifth of the major seventh by a semitone. It is the augmented triad with a major seventh above it.
chords.maj7b5: The major seventh flat five lowers the fifth of the major seventh. It is a near relative of the major seventh and the major flat five.
chords.b5: The major flat five is a major triad with its fifth lowered a semitone. It keeps the major third, so the sound still reads as major, and the three notes repeat across the neck. Its nearest relatives are the major triad and the diminished triad.
chords.dim: The diminished triad stacks two minor thirds, giving a root, a minor third and a flat five. It is a compact, symmetrical shape that tends to repeat at regular distances on the neck. Add a seventh and it becomes the diminished seventh or the half diminished chord.
chords.dim7: The diminished seventh stacks three minor thirds, so its four notes divide the octave into equal parts. That symmetry means the same shape can be named from four different roots, and it repeats at regular steps along the neck. It is the fully symmetrical sibling of the half diminished chord.
chords.m7b5: The half diminished chord is a diminished triad with a minor seventh, so it keeps the flat five of the diminished chord but not its seventh. It shares its notes with a minor sixth chord built a minor third higher, so the two shapes overlap on the neck. It sits between the minor seventh and the diminished seventh.
chords.mb5: The minor flat five is another listing of the diminished triad, a root with a minor third and a flat fifth. The three notes repeat across the neck in compact shapes. Its relatives are the minor triad and the half diminished chord.
chords.aug: The augmented triad stacks two major thirds, so its three notes divide the octave evenly. That symmetry means the same shape recurs along the neck, and it can be named from any of its three notes. It sits one semitone away from the major triad, with a raised fifth.
chords.s5: The augmented fifth is the major triad with its fifth raised a semitone, the same notes as the augmented triad listed under a different name. The three notes divide the octave evenly, so the shape repeats along the neck. It is a neighbour of the major triad and the seventh sharp five.

scales.major: The major scale is seven notes in a pattern of whole and half steps, and it is the reference most other scales are compared with. On the neck its notes cover most of the fretboard, and patterns slide along a few connected shapes. Its modes are the same notes starting from a different degree.
scales.ionian: The Ionian scale has the same notes as the major scale and is the first of the seven modes. On the neck it is the shape that other modes are measured from. Shift the starting note and the same positions become Dorian, Phrygian and the rest.
scales.dorian: The Dorian mode is a minor scale with a raised sixth, the second mode of the major scale. It uses the same notes as a major scale a whole step below, so the neck shows one shape under two names. It sits between the natural minor and the major scale in colour.
scales.phrygian: The Phrygian mode is the third mode of the major scale, a minor scale with a lowered second. That lowered second sits a semitone above the root on the neck. It shares its notes with a major scale a major third below.
scales.lydian: The Lydian mode is the fourth mode of the major scale, a major scale with a raised fourth. The raised fourth sits a tritone from the root, and the scale shares its notes with a major scale a fifth above. It is the brightest of the seven modes.
scales.mixolydian: The Mixolydian mode is a major scale with a lowered seventh, the fifth mode of the major scale. It shares its notes with a major scale a fifth below, so one set of positions serves both. It is the scale that fits the dominant seventh chord.
scales.aeolian: The Aeolian mode is the natural minor scale, the sixth mode of the major scale. It shares its notes with the major scale a minor third above, so the neck shows one shape with two names. Its close relatives are the harmonic and melodic minor scales.
scales.locrian: The Locrian mode is the seventh mode of the major scale, with a lowered second and a lowered fifth. The lowered fifth takes away the stable fifth above the root, so it sounds unsettled. It shares its notes with a major scale a semitone above.
scales.harmonic-minor: The harmonic minor scale is the natural minor with a raised seventh, which leaves a gap of three semitones between the sixth and seventh degrees. That gap is easy to spot on the neck as a wider step. It sits between the natural minor and the melodic minor scale.
scales.harmonic-major: The harmonic major scale is the major scale with a lowered sixth. That change creates a wide step between the sixth and seventh degrees, in the same place as the harmonic minor gap. It is the major counterpart of the harmonic minor.
scales.melodic-minor-ascending: The ascending melodic minor scale is a minor scale with a raised sixth and seventh, so only the third marks it as minor. On the neck it looks like a major scale with one note lowered. Its descending form returns to the natural minor.
scales.pentatonic-minor: The minor pentatonic scale has five notes, the root, a minor third, a fourth, a fifth and a minor seventh. It is a subset of the natural minor, so its shapes sit inside the larger scale on the neck. Add a flat five and you reach the blues scale.
scales.pentatonic-major: The major pentatonic scale has five notes, the root, a second, a third, a fifth and a sixth. It shares its notes with the minor pentatonic a minor third lower, so the same boxes serve both. It is a subset of the major scale with the fourth and seventh left out.
scales.pentatonic-blues: This blues scale adds a flattened fifth to the minor pentatonic, giving six notes. That extra note sits between the fourth and the fifth, so on the neck it fills the gap in the minor pentatonic box. It is the six note blues entry in the library.
scales.blues: The blues scale listed here has six notes, with a raised fourth between the fourth and the fifth. The map shows how that one extra note joins the minor pentatonic shapes on the neck. It is a close relative of the minor pentatonic.
scales.whole-tone: The whole tone scale has six notes, each a whole step from the next. Because every step is equal, the same shape repeats along the neck at regular distances, and only two different versions exist. It has no half steps, so it differs from every mode of the major scale.
scales.chromatic: The chromatic scale uses all twelve notes, each a semitone from the next. On the neck it simply fills every fret, so the map has no gaps. Every other scale in the library is a selection from it.
scales.octatonic-h-w: This eight note scale alternates a half step and a whole step. Its pattern repeats every three frets, so the same shape recurs along the neck. It is the half then whole form, and the whole then half form is its sibling.
scales.octatonic-w-h: This eight note scale alternates a whole step and a half step. Its pattern repeats every three frets, so the shape recurs along the neck. It contains the notes of diminished seventh chords and is the sibling of the half then whole form.
scales.double-harmonic: The double harmonic scale has a lowered second and a lowered sixth, which makes two wide steps of three semitones. Both gaps are easy to see on the neck as stretched intervals around the third and the seventh. It is a major scale with those two notes lowered.
scales.hirajoshi: The Hirajoshi scale is a five note scale built from wide and narrow steps. It has no seventh and gives the neck a spare, open outline. It is a close relative of the Kumoi and Pelog scales in the library.
scales.kumoi: The Kumoi scale has five notes, the root, a second, a minor third, a fifth and a sixth. It has no fourth and no seventh, so on the neck it sits as a compact, open five note shape.
scales.neapolitan: The Neapolitan scale is a minor scale with a lowered second and a natural seventh. The lowered second sits a semitone above the root, and the raised seventh sits a semitone below it. On the neck both sit right beside the root.
scales.hungarian-minor: The Hungarian minor scale is a minor scale with a raised fourth and a natural seventh. It has two wide steps, one around the fourth and one around the sixth and seventh. The map makes both stretches easy to find.
scales.spanish-gypsy: The Spanish Gypsy scale is a major scale with a lowered second, a lowered sixth and a lowered seventh. It keeps the major third above a lowered second, so a wide step sits right at the start. It is the Phrygian mode with a raised third.
scales.pentatonic-neutral: The neutral pentatonic scale has five notes and no third at all, so it is neither major nor minor. It holds a second, a fourth, a fifth and a minor seventh, which gives the neck an open, ambiguous outline. It is a spare relative of the major and minor pentatonic scales.

tunings.standard: Standard tuning runs E A D G B E from the lowest string to the highest, mostly in fourths with one major third between the G and the B. That one irregular gap is why chord shapes change when they cross it. Most fretboard maps you meet assume this tuning first.
tunings.d-standard: D Standard tunes every string of standard tuning down a whole step, giving D G C F A D. Every shape keeps its form and only the note names move. It is the simplest way to lower the pitch of a whole instrument.
tunings.c-standard: C Standard lowers every string a further whole step from D Standard, giving C F A# D# G C. The strings keep standard tuning's relationships, so shapes carry over unchanged. Only the note names slide down.
tunings.drop-d: Drop D lowers the lowest string of standard tuning by a whole step, giving D A D G B E. The bottom three strings now sit in fifths and fourths, so a power chord is a straight bar across them. The other five strings are unchanged.
tunings.drop-c: Drop C is C G C F A D, D Standard with its lowest string dropped a further step. It repeats the Drop D relationship a step lower, so the bottom three strings are a straight bar for a power chord. The upper five strings match those of D Standard.
tunings.drop-a: Drop A is A A D G B E, with the lowest string lowered to match the second string an octave below. The two lowest strings share a note, so the bottom of the neck holds an octave. The top four strings are standard.
tunings.double-drop-d: Double Drop D is D A D G B D, lowering both outer strings of standard tuning by a whole step. The two D strings sit two octaves apart. The inner four strings keep their standard relationships.
tunings.open-a: Open A is E A E A C# E, tuned so that the open strings sound an A major chord. A single finger across the neck makes a chord anywhere. The map shows how that same shape moves with the fret.
tunings.open-a-minor: Open A Minor is E A E A C E, tuned so that the open strings sound an A minor chord. One barre across the neck gives a minor chord at every fret. It differs from Open A by a single string.
tunings.open-c: Open C is C G C G C E, tuned so that the open strings sound a C major chord. Fifths and octaves fill the lower strings and a major third sits on top. A barre makes a major chord at every fret.
tunings.open-c6: Open C6 is C G C G A E, adding a sixth to the Open C chord. The open strings sound a C sixth chord, and the sixth sits on the second string. It is a one string change from Open C.
tunings.open-d: Open D is D A D F# A D, tuned so that the open strings sound a D major chord. The map shows the same barre idea as the other open major tunings. A barre across the neck makes a major chord at every fret.
tunings.open-d-minor: Open D Minor is D A D F A D, the Open D tuning with its third lowered. The open strings sound a D minor chord. It differs from Open D by a single string.
tunings.open-d5: Open D5 is D A D D A D, a tuning with no third at all. The open strings give only roots and fifths, so a barre makes a power chord at every fret and the major or minor colour comes from the notes you add.
tunings.open-e: Open E is E B E G# B E, tuned so that the open strings sound an E major chord. It is Open D raised a whole step, so the shapes match. A barre makes a major chord at every fret.
tunings.open-g: Open G is D G D G B D, tuned so that the open strings sound a G major chord. The map shows how a barre across any fret gives a major chord. It is the open tuning most players meet first.
tunings.open-g-dobro: Open G Dobro is G B D G B D, so the open strings sound a G major chord with the root on both the lowest and the fourth string. Compared with Open G, the lowest two strings are higher. It is the usual tuning for resonator guitars.
tunings.open-g-minor: Open G Minor is D G D G A# D, the Open G tuning with its third lowered. The open strings sound a G minor chord. It differs from Open G by one string.
tunings.open-g6: Open G6 is D G D G B E, the Open G tuning with the highest string raised to a sixth. The open strings sound a G sixth chord. It differs from Open G by one string.
tunings.celtic: Celtic, or DADGAD, is D A D G A D, a tuning with no third in the open strings. The open strings hold roots, fourths and fifths, so the sound is neither major nor minor until you add a note. The map shows the shapes that arise from this ambiguity.
tunings.low-c: Low C is C G D G A D, lowering several strings of standard tuning to open a low register. The open strings span a wide range of pitches. Its upper three strings match those of DADGAD.
tunings.all-fourths: All Fourths is E A D G C F, replacing the major third of standard tuning with a fourth. Every pair of adjacent strings is now the same distance apart, so any shape moves up and down the neck unchanged. The map becomes regular in a way standard tuning is not.
tunings.nst: New Standard Tuning is C G D A E G, mostly fifths with a minor third between the top two strings. The wide spacing gives a large range across the neck. The map shows how the strings repeat notes across the fretboard.
tunings.baritone: Baritone tuning is B E A D F# B, standard tuning lowered by a fourth. It keeps the same relationships, so familiar shapes carry over unchanged. Only the note names move.
tunings.seven-standard: Seven String Standard is B E A D G B E, adding a low B to standard tuning. The six upper strings keep their familiar spacing. The new string extends the range below the low E.
tunings.seven-drop-a: Seven String Drop A is A E A D G B E, lowering the low B of seven string standard by a whole step. The two lowest strings now sit a fifth apart, which makes a power chord a one finger shape. The upper six strings are standard.
tunings.bass-4: Bass four string tuning is E A D G, all in fourths, matching the lowest four strings of a guitar an octave lower. Every adjacent pair of strings is the same distance apart. The map uses the same shapes as the guitar but spaced across a longer neck.
tunings.bass-5: Bass five string tuning is B E A D G, adding a low B below the four string bass. All five strings sit in fourths. The added string extends the range below the low E.
tunings.ukulele: Ukulele tuning is G C E A with a reentrant top string, meaning the G is higher than the C and E below it. Because the strings are not in order of pitch, the map looks different from guitar tunings. The shapes are small, since it uses only four strings.
tunings.ukulele-low-g: Ukulele with a low G is G C E A, the same letters as reentrant tuning but with the G an octave lower. The strings now run in order from low to high. The map shows how this changes the shapes compared with the reentrant tuning.

families.chord:triads: A triad stacks three notes: a root, a third and a fifth. Major, minor, diminished and augmented triads differ only in which thirds and fifths they use. Every larger chord on this site is built on one of them.
families.chord:power-and-suspended: These chords leave out the third or swap it for a neighbour. The power chord is only a root and a fifth, while suspended chords replace the third with a second or a fourth. None of them sounds major or minor on its own.
families.chord:sixths-and-added: These chords add one colour note to a triad without reaching up to a seventh. A sixth or a ninth sits on top of the major or minor triad underneath. The fretboard shows where each added note falls across the neck.
families.chord:sevenths: Seventh chords add a fourth note a seventh above the root. Dominant, major, minor, minor major, diminished and half diminished sevenths each use a different seventh over a different triad. They are the usual starting point for chord progressions beyond the triad.
families.chord:extended: Extended chords stack thirds past the seventh to reach the ninth, eleventh or thirteenth. Few players sound every note at once, so the fretboard marks which tones are optional. Each one is built on a seventh chord below it.
families.chord:altered: Altered dominants raise or lower the ninth of a dominant seventh chord. The sharp nine and the flat nine each add tension that asks to resolve. The map shows where those altered tones sit against the rest of the chord.
families.scale:major-and-modes: The major scale and the six modes that start from its other degrees share the same seven notes. Each mode simply begins on a different one, which changes where the tonal centre sits. The map shows them side by side for any root.
families.scale:pentatonic-and-blues: Pentatonic scales keep five notes of a seven note scale, and the blues scale adds one passing note to the minor pentatonic. They are small enough to learn as a few shapes across the neck. The map shows every position of each one.
families.scale:minor-scales: Harmonic and melodic minor change the natural minor scale by raising one or two of its notes. The raised notes create the leading tone that natural minor lacks. The map shows how those changes alter the pattern across the neck.
families.index: Every board on With Handlebars is one chord or scale on one tuning, shown across the whole neck. Browse them by tuning, by chord family or by scale family, then open a board to see and hear its notes. Each page lists its neighbours so you can move sideways.
